raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old, Middle-Eastern male was admitted with a high fever, chills, and vomiting. The symptoms had begun while he was in Liberia, and he came back to Syria as soon as his fever worsened. The patient had no other clinical symptoms and no medical history of other illnesses or drug consumption.
A blood test was performed, and a blood smear was examined under the light microscope (Table 1). He was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum, and the test was run twice in two different labs. The patient was treated accordingly with artemisinin, 4 tablets per dose twice a day for three days (each tablet contains 20 mg artemether and 120 mg lumefantrine).
Twenty days after malaria treatment, the patient continued to suffer from fever, shivers, and general fatigue. Clinical presentation included pale skin, mucosa, and right hypochondriac pain without jaundice. A blood test with further lab examinations was performed (Table 2).
Blood smears were run for three consecutive days to detect Plasmodium falciparum organisms, while a computed tomography (CT) scan and abdominal echography were also scheduled.
The smears returned negative, and the CT scan revealed liver abscesses (Figures 1 and 2); thus, further tests were required.
A blood test was performed searching for Echinococcus granulosus antibodies and Entamoeba histolytica antibodies, and the test rendered positive results for Entamoeba histolytica.
The abscess was drained as a therapeutic and diagnostic measure, followed by a course of 500 mg intravenous metronidazole every 8 hours for 14 days (Flagyl), to complete the treatment. After improvement, the patient was discharged and instructed to contact his physician if any of his symptoms relapsed, which did not occur.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old Middle-Eastern male presented with high fever, chills, and vomiting that began in Liberia, followed 20 days after malaria treatment by persistent fever, shivers, general fatigue, and right hypochondriac pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high fever, chills, and vomiting while in Liberia and returned to Syria as soon as his fever worsened. He was initially diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria on blood smear (confirmed twice in two different laboratories) and treated with artemisinin combination therapy (4 tablets twice daily for 3 days, each tablet containing 20 mg artemether and 120 mg lumefantrine). Twenty days after completing malaria therapy, he continued to experience persistent fever, shivers, general fatigue, and right hypochondriac pain without jaundice.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history of other illnesses. Recent travel history to Liberia prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, shivers, vomiting, general fatigue, and right hypochondriac pain. Negative for other clinical symptoms, jaundice, or prior drug consumption.

objective.physical_examination: Pale skin and mucosa, and right hypochondriac pain without jaundice.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial peripheral blood smear under light microscopy was positive for Plasmodium falciparum (confirmed in two laboratories). Repeat blood smears performed for 3 consecutive days (20 days post-malaria treatment) were negative for Plasmodium falciparum. Further blood tests and abdominal echography were performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed liver abscesses. Therapeutic and diagnostic drainage of the liver abscess was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serological blood testing for Entamoeba histolytica and Echinococcus granulosus antibodies returned positive for Entamoeba histolytica antibodies and negative for Echinococcus granulosus, confirming a final diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess following treated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (with repeat malaria smears ruled out). The patient underwent therapeutic and diagnostic abscess drainage followed by intravenous metronidazole (Flagyl) 500 mg every 8 hours for 14 days. He improved, was discharged with instructions to return if symptoms relapsed, and experienced no recurrence.
